idiom_name: cursor struct (source handle, buffer, position) plus bool next(Cursor *, T *)
implementation_notes: C has no laziness primitive, so the lazy collection is a struct that owns the source state and a step function that produces exactly one element per call and reports exhaustion by returning false; the consumer's loop owns demand and can stop at any element, which keeps an unbounded or larger-than-memory source at constant memory. The classic hand-written cursor is also the right choice when the position must be inspectable, resumable or serialisable, and it works on freestanding toolchains where no coroutine machinery exists.
pitfalls: A cursor that owns a FILE*, buffer or handle leaks it unless the caller (or a matching destroy function) releases it - C has no finalizers, and an abandoned lazy sequence is exactly the case garbage-collected languages get for free.
Copying the cursor struct by value duplicates buffered state and the file position; lazy sequences must be passed by pointer (or be documented as non-copyable).
Buffered steps such as fgets truncate very long lines and stop at embedded NUL bytes, so a lazy line source can silently change the element stream.

variants.name: Stackful coroutine producer (ucontext or protothreads)
variants.implementation_notes: Instead of a hand-rolled state machine, the producer can be written as ordinary sequential code and suspended at each element: POSIX ucontext (getcontext/makecontext/swapcontext) gives each generator its own stack, while Dunkels protothreads are a stackless, macro-based variant that compiles to a state machine and therefore works in interrupt handlers. Use it when the producing logic is complex enough that a hand-written cursor becomes unmaintainable; keep the cursor when portability, stack budget or context-switch cost dominate.
pitfalls: ucontext is POSIX, not ISO C: it is unavailable on some platforms (and deprecated on macOS), and a context switch inside a signal handler or with a shared stack is undefined behaviour.
Each stackful coroutine needs its own stack; thousands of live lazy sequences multiply the memory that laziness was supposed to save.
Protothreads cannot be suspended from inside nested function calls (no real stack), so helper functions must be inlined via macros or the producer is split artificially.
